title: Russell Brand: Alleged rape victim wants age of consent law changed
description: Warning - this story contains graphic contentA woman who has alleged that she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 has waived her right to anony
body: Warning - this story contains graphic contentA woman who has alleged that she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 has waived her right to anonymity and is campaigning for a staggered age of consent in an interview with the Sunday Times.Mia Latter was one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation. She was known under the pseudonym 'Alice'. Brand denied the allegations at the time.None of the women in the 2023 media investigation were complainants in Brand's recent criminal trial.On Monday the entertainer was sentenced to 10 and a half years for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was acquitted of two counts of rape and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.The Sunday Times reported that Latter had initially described the allegation about Brand to them as a sexual assault and that is how they reported it in their 2023 investigation.Latter, 37, "now calls this allegation rape", the paper said.Latter said she was 16 when she met Brand, who was 30 at the time, when she was on her way home from a shopping trip. She said Brand was working at MTV.She told the paper: "I think people were so struck by my story because of the age difference and the clear imbalance [in power],"She said Brand told her to keep their relationship secret from her school friends and claimed that he referred to her as "the child" in front of his entourage.It was towards the end of their relationship that Latter was allegedly orally raped by Brand, according to the Sunday Times.Latter said that she was now campaigning for the introduction of a "staggered" age of consent that would prohibit relationships between 16- and 17-year-olds and adults."I don't want to criminalise teenagers having sex with each other," she told the paper. "If you're between the ages of 16 and 18, it seems reasonable that you can have relationships with each other, and [teenagers] are always going to. But … if you're in your thirties, forties and fifties and you're trying to have a relationship with someone under the age of 18, it [should be] a criminal offence."She also told the paper that she would not continue with the criminal process so she could focus on her campaign.In her interview with the Sunday Times she said that the CPS decided not to include her as part of Brand's criminal trial but the police wanted her to be part of a "subsequent trial".A Met Police spokesperson said: "Officers launched an investigation in January 2026 after receiving an allegation of rape."Detectives sought advice from the Crown Prosecution Service to determine how best to proceed, and officers were advised that further information was needed before a charging decision could be made."This investigation remains ongoing. We understand the delay has been distressing for this victim-survivor. However, our focus has been on putting forward the best possible evidence."A spokesperson for the Crown Prosecution Service said it would "continue to work closely with investigators to provide advice and make sure cases progress as quickly as possible".

schema.headline: Russell Brand: Alleged rape victim wants age of consent law changed

title: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
description: US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, Presid
body: US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.The US has not confirmed Zelensky's comments, and a US official told the BBC "many ideas continue to be discussed but any final deal will have to be agreed to by both parties".The Ukrainian leader's comments came after US envoys met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelensky as part of US efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance, but this has previously been opposed by the US and others while Russia has said another Nato member on its border is unacceptable.Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. It controls most of the industrial region of Donbas and Zelensky has consistently said Ukraine is unwilling to give up sovereign territory."The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky said in remarks released by his office on Saturday.He went on to say that if he received a specific proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital, Dublin, on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Putin in Moscow.Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted. It has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.Ukraine has rejected these, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.Other Nato members apart from the US are wary of membership for Ukraine - and it is understood that Ukraine itself sees that as unrealistic. The Kremlin has always been fiercely opposed, too. It is one reason why Russia started this war in the first place.It is possible the American envoys were exploring Ukraine's "red lines" when it comes to occupied land in the Donbas. Zelensky said recently that the US mediators believed Kyiv only had to cede territory to achieve peace and were applying pressure, keen to do a deal as soon as possible.Ukraine is sure that Russia's ambitions are far greater and has long seen Nato as its only sure protection.So it is also possible that Zelensky made this suggestion public in order to re-open a discussion that had been considered all but closed.He maintains that the idea is now "back on the agenda" as part of an "extremely difficult conversation" on European security.It also looks like Ukrainian push-back against Russia's renewed hardline stance. Moscow now talks about a "new European security architecture", which is long-standing Russian code for a weaker Nato.The issue appears to have been the main focus at the latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi this week.Hours after Zelensky's remarks, Jared Kushner appeared keen to dampen down any US offer of Nato membership for Ukraine, urging "confidentiality" in a sensitive process.He said that "maximalist" proposals had been reported from the negotiations, along with "strong political rhetoric".In what read like a reproach to Kyiv, Kushner referred to "private discussions" aimed at exploring new ideas about ending what he called a "horrible war".He said the hope was that those ideas might lead to new proposals or breakthroughs.Russia currently occupies roughly a fifth of Ukrainian territory, including most of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions that compose the Donbas. It has insisted again that it will not agree to a ceasefire until a final peace deal is in place that would include Ukraine ceding control of those parts of the Donbas Russian troops have not captured, in addition to the Crimean peninsula Moscow annexed illegally in 2014.The latest round of talks come after a period of fraught relations between Kyiv and Washington over Ukrainian strikes on oil facilities deep inside Russia, which Trump had asked Ukraine to pause to facilitate the supply of Russian diesel to ease global fuel prices.Zelensky then accused US officials of limiting Ukraine's Starlink internet service, which it uses to co-ordinate defensive operations, while Trump said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president" and called for fresh elections.Elections are suspended while Ukraine remains under martial law, but Zelensky has previously said he was willing to hold them within months of a peace deal being reached and would give up the presidency in exchange for Nato membership.

schema.headline: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says

title: Pope Leo speaks on community 'suffering' on visit to remote Andes
description: Cajamarca has lost the highest number of people to internal migration, with 729,000 people born there now living elsewhere in Peru.In his sermon, Pope
body: Cajamarca has lost the highest number of people to internal migration, with 729,000 people born there now living elsewhere in Peru.In his sermon, Pope Leo thanked those who had made the journey to him and emphasised the importance of never losing heart, despite life's difficulties.Santa Cruz is within the Diocese of Chiclayo, where Pope Leo served as bishop from 2015 to 2023. During his tenure, he visited Santa Cruz several times a year to minister to the town's rural population.On Saturday he returned by helicopter, where he was greeted by singing and cheering. He later did a tour in a popemobile, where he waved to people who had travelled from across the region to see him.Speaking at a local parish on Saturday, the Pope said he felt "joy" at being able to visit the small town once again."It is like a very big dream that the Lord has allowed this servant to come here," he said.Rev. Kevin Noriega, who was ordained in 2018 by the then-bishop, told Reuters the visit had brought "enormous hope and emotion" to Santa Cruz. He said: "People are eager to experience this Holy Mass ... because after so much time they will be able to see their bishop - 'Father Robert,' as they used to call him - now as the Holy Father."

schema.headline: Pope Leo speaks on community 'suffering' on visit to remote Andes

title: Bletchley Park officer's Aston Martin DB5 to be sold at auction
description: An Aston Martin car owned by a British intelligence officer, and of the same model made famous by the James Bond films, is expected to fetch up to £40
body: An Aston Martin car owned by a British intelligence officer, and of the same model made famous by the James Bond films, is expected to fetch up to £400,000 when it goes to auction.The red Aston Martin DB5 Sports Saloon car will go on sale at Sandown Park in Esher, Surrey.It was owned by PH Manners Wood, who interpreted decoded enigma messages at Bletchley Park during World War Two, and who bought the car in the same year Bond first hit the big screen.Paul Cheetham, of auctioneers H&H Classics, said: "James Bond was not the only British intelligence officer to take delivery of an Aston Martin DB5 during 1964, as seen with this wonderful example first owned by Manners Wood."He added that the car had "links to a real British hero who, along with his colleagues, made such a difference to help end the hostilities in the Second World War".The Aston Martin DB5 has also become synonymous with the Bond films thanks to its use in movies such as Goldfinger alongside Sean Connery, and Skyfall with Daniel Craig's 007.The next James Bond film is currently reported to be casting its new lead, with speculation as to which actor will take up the mantle.Manners Wood's rare DB5 is among just under 900 of the cars to be produced and has had two owners since, including its current owner who has looked after it for 56 years, according to H&H Classics.The intelligence officer worked at Bletchley Park and was credited with saving thousands of lives by General Dwight D Eisenhower, later to become US president.H&H Classics says the DB5 will go on display at Sandown Park on 9 December, ahead of the auction the following day.Follow BBC Surrey on Facebook, external, on X, external, and on Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Surrey on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk, external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.

schema.headline: Bletchley Park officer's Aston Martin DB5 to be sold at auction

title: Wales 35-28 New Zealand: The magical day Wales beat the All Blacks again
description: One of the greatest Wales wins of all time.That is how former captain Sam Warburton described the monumental result against New Zealand in Cardiff on
body: One of the greatest Wales wins of all time.That is how former captain Sam Warburton described the monumental result against New Zealand in Cardiff on Saturday.At the time of the kick-off, the All Blacks were effectively the top-ranked side in the world following South Africa's tension-filled loss to France on Friday night.So no-one gave Wales a glimmer of hope - even Warburton - with some bookmakers offering odds of 30-1 during the week.The question, not of when but can Wales beat the All Blacks again has beset them since 1953.That 73-year wait has been marred by cheating, national scandal and pure sporting drama.Little wonder then that few wanted to leave the Principality Stadium long after the final whistle had sparked unprecedented scenes of utter joy, tears and relief to the strains of Yma O Hyd. The outpouring of unbridled emotion after a losing run - stretching across 34 matches - that has hung like a millstone around the necks of generations of Wales players.Warburton himself was part of one of the most successful teams of all time during the Warren Gatland era - but lost all five meetings with New Zealand.Even the legendary team of the 1970s fell short, although Sir Gareth Edwards was among the smallest Principality Stadium crowd for a Wales-New Zealand fixture to witness history. How many more will claim in years to come that they were there as well?Wales had only come close on a handful of occasions with one-point defeats in 1978, when New Zealand lock Andy Haden infamously dived out of a lineout to gain a match-winning penalty, and then in 2004.Wales even turned to four New Zealand coaches in Sir Graham Henry, Steve Hansen, Gatland and Wayne Pivac to help break the hoodoo, but none of the quartet could inspire a Test victory over the land of their birth.So there will be added satisfaction that it was a Welshman who masterminded the long-awaited win.Steve Tandy's side may not have the household names of teams gone by, nor the winning pedigree, but they had courage when it mattered.Three times they held up black shirts over the try-line during a second-half defensive effort that at times beggared belief.Initial statistics had second-row Dafydd Jenkins equalling Thierry Dusautoir's world record of 38 tackles in a single match - also set against New Zealand in 2007.Jac Morgan and man of the match James Botham also topped 30 tackles, while centre Eddie James and captain Dewi Lake were not far behind.It earned high praise from former New Zealand captain Sean Fitzpatrick.A winner in all six meetings with Wales, the ex-hooker has ties to that day seven decades ago when his father Brian made his New Zealand debut.Observers say he was unlucky not to be awarded a try after he was adjudged to have been tackled just short of the line. How different history might have been."New Zealand played well in patches and terrible in others but this is all about Wales," said Fitzpatrick, now a board member of Welsh region Scarlets."The way they started the game and took their tries showed the amazing belief they had. But the defensive effort was out of this world."

schema.headline: Wales 35-28 New Zealand: The magical day Wales beat the All Blacks again

title: England 78-15 Japan: Will Joseph makes sensational Test comeback
description: Eddie Jones aired a complaint about Twickenham's in-stadium experience when he appeared on BBC Radio 5 Live this week."Being a spectator and being tol
body: Eddie Jones aired a complaint about Twickenham's in-stadium experience when he appeared on BBC Radio 5 Live this week."Being a spectator and being told when to make noise is a bit funny," said the Japan boss, objecting to a big-screen request for an increase in volume.Jones sat stony-faced in the coaching box as the message appeared again in the midst of his team's 78-15 thrashing at England's hands on Saturday.There was little for him to enjoy on his return to Twickenham, where he was head coach for seven years.But, for the rest of a capacity crowd, it was a fun one.With junior tickets on sale at £15, there was a different atmosphere from usual. The decibels were higher, the demographic was younger, the spirits a little lighter.And England brought plenty of entertainment to the party. Thirteen tries in total, with Will Joseph's five putting him in the centre of the chorus line.The 24-year-old won his only previous England cap under Jones. Back in the summer of 2022, he was a teenage apprentice taken on tour to Australia and thrust into the second Test as a last-minute replacement.His promise has taken some time to be fulfilled. He struggled for game time and fitness at Harlequins after London Irish's bankruptcy forced him to move on from his boyhood club.An auto-immune condition that cost him the hearing in his left ear was one setback at the Stoop.But, as part of a rat pack of exciting young English-qualified backs at Gloucester this season, he has been superb: a swerving, offloading, game-breaking threat either on the wing or in midfield.England deployed him out wide, to bring some of the razzle-dazzle that they lost as Immanuel Feyi-Waboso limped out of their autumn campaign.Reports from Pennyhill Park during the week had suggested Joseph was doing a fine job of replicating Feyi-Waboso's explosive elusiveness.He certainly did on Twickenham's main stage, finishing chances with the same pace and power."He is pretty similar to Immanuel Feyi-Waboso in the way he plays his game," said former England wing Chris Ashton on BBC Radio 5 Live."He is just so fast. He doesn't look too fast in the first two steps and then he is just gone. He gets away from people."Joseph's cartwheeling plant of the ball over the line for his fourth summed up his exuberance.In the aftermath of that score, Japan flanker Ben Gunter put a consoling arm around full-back Kazuma Ueda, who had been comprehensively burned in a race to the corner.Japan couldn't get near Joseph, whose first try came after just 60 seconds and his hat-trick score in the 19th minute."It has been a challenging four years, but I have enjoyed the journey to get back here and I am happy all that hard work I have put in has paid off," he said."I have had a taste for it now and I can't wait to do it again."We have been here before though.There was another teenage apprentice taken on that tour of Australia alongside Joseph.Henry Arundell was Joseph's Irish team-mate. His impact on the trip was greater, scoring a try in the first Test and winning his second and third caps in the series.The following year, while Joseph returned to the club scene, Arundell made his first England start in the Six Nations.He earned a place in the Rugby World Cup squad and, in a foregone conclusion of a pool match, cantered in for five tries against Chile in Lille.Arundell was electric against limited opposition. He has yet to convince in sterner Tests.Joseph still has those to come. A shade slower, but a smidge smarter, he may be better suited to the Test scene.New Zealand next Saturday, stung by defeat by Wales, would definitely be a step up if Steve Borthwick decides to find out.There was plenty elsewhere to please the head coach.George Martin was at his abrasive best. The Saracens second row led England's carry and tackle standings in the comeback performance we have been waiting for since his 14-month injury lay-off ended in May.Ellis Genge was snorting fire and bruising ribs and Maro Itoje's rejuvenation after a summer off continues.In the backline, Max Ojomoh was too clever and quick for the Japanese midfield, spotting space either for himself or others.Henry Pollock, the other point of interest in a much-changed line-up, found it harder to get into the game with ball in hand, but did the dirty work in defence and at the breakdown that some have questioned.Borthwick will be waiting nervously on news from his medical room this week, with Ollie Chessum, Seb Atkinson and George Furbank hoping to return in time for the All Blacks.But a fourth win in a row, after five successive defeats, has further buoyed up his regime."The team is really starting to play well," he told BBC 5 Live. "The speed and positioning in attack was very good which gave us options to be able to move the ball."There was intent to play fast, with all the strengths of English rugby. We've got some really great attacking talent and I think we are seeing that."The balance of pass-kick decisions was really good. Ultimately I think one of the main things is the supporters really enjoyed it. The atmosphere was excellent."Even Jones, who had Borthwick as an assistant during a previous stint with Japan and his time with England, managed a smile by the end."It kills me that Will Joseph, I gave him his first cap, he scores five tries against me. Now that's not being very loyal, is it?," he joked."He's a great kid. He always was going to be a good player."England will hope he might turn out even better than that.

schema.headline: England 78-15 Japan: Will Joseph makes sensational Test comeback

title: New Orleans port sues tanker owners over cruise ship collision for $1m
description: The paddlewheel cruise ship, American Heritage, was left on its side and partially submerged in the Mississippi River after it was hit by the cargo ve
body: The paddlewheel cruise ship, American Heritage, was left on its side and partially submerged in the Mississippi River after it was hit by the cargo vessel Atlantic Asphalt on Friday afternoon.The court documents added that the port terminal "was significantly damaged" in the incident.The tanker, the M/V Atlantic Asphalt, its owner Nave Shipping SA, and its management company, Thome Ship Management Pte Ltd, are all named in the federal court lawsuit filed on Friday in the Eastern District of Louisiana court. Officials are still investigating the full extent of the damage from the crash, as well as the cause, but the lawsuit says the port is looking for money to cover cleanup, inspections, repairs and other expenses.The lawsuit requests that the tanker be seized and sold to pay for the damage. It also alleges that the collision "occurred as a result of the negligence, gross negligence, fault or carelessness" of the ship and operating companies.It alleges that the tanker and companies failed "to use all available means to avoid the risk" of colliding with the riverboat. Nave Shipping is a subsidiary of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation. BBC has contacted the China State Shipbuilding Corporation for comment. Thome Ship Management has also been contacted. The firm said in a statement on Saturday that the crew of the Atlantic Asphalt were safe and accounted for."OSM Thome is fully complying with the local authorities as they carry out the necessary investigations," it said.There were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, on the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to the port authority.Tugboat operators, police and other rescuers rushed to help while officials shut down traffic in the Mississippi River during the rescue effort.The American Heritage had been finishing an eight-day cruise calling at destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi along the waterway.

schema.headline: New Orleans port sues tanker owners over cruise ship collision for $1m

title: I took Vinted to court to get my money back
description: Mali Osmelak never imagined that selling clothes on Vinted would end with a court claim to recover almost £6,000.She started trading on the platform t
body: Mali Osmelak never imagined that selling clothes on Vinted would end with a court claim to recover almost £6,000.She started trading on the platform to earn an income while managing Crohn's disease and caring for her four-year-old daughter.But when she became a professional seller in March, she was unable to complete Vinted's verification process, leaving thousands of pounds inaccessible in her Vinted wallet. After several weeks of trying to resolve the issue, Mali took legal action. Vinted says sellers may be asked to complete verification checks to comply with legal and regulatory requirements and 98% of transactions are completed smoothly without needing help from its support team.Vinted is hugely popular in the UK with 17 million users. The online marketplace does not charge a fee to sellers for listing on there.After the BBC reported on users whose accounts had been suspended or banned, dozens of people got in touch describing difficulties accessing money held in their Vinted wallets.Mali joined Vinted in 2024 as a side-hustle. Demand for her second-hand gymwear grew rapidly and, within months, she had set up a limited company to expand the business.This year she signed up for a Vinted Pro seller account - designed for people who want to sell a high volume of items and who are registered as a business.Within weeks she had generated almost £6,000 in sales. But when she tried to withdraw the money, she discovered her account had been restricted and was told she needed to complete a verification process."I thought, 'That's OK. It's not rocket science,'" she says. "I'd set up the business with the help of an accountant and had all the information they needed."Mali says she spotted an error Vinted had made with her name and she flagged it with Vinted, but "again nothing was done and the verification kept failing". She found herself stuck in a cycle of automated responses.  In an effort to break the deadlock, she also contacted Mangopay, the payments company that at the time operated Vinted sellers' wallets and processed transactions on the platform. She was directed back to Vinted.After eight weeks without access to the money, Mali decided to take both companies to the small claims court, spending £455 in court fees.Three days after the court claim was filed, Mali says the account was "magically verified" and she could withdraw the funds.She still pressed ahead with the case though to try to recover her court fees, costs and interest. In June, she obtained a default judgement after neither Vinted nor Mangopay responded to her claim, with the court ordering the companies to pay £1,207.50.But she has yet to receive the money. She has since been informed that Vinted and Mangopay have applied to have the judgement set aside, with a hearing scheduled for December."It's been ridiculous and incredibly stressful," she says."I need that cash. I will fight it. I'm going to tell the court their system is completely broken. I needed help and nobody helped me."Vinted said: "Ms Osmelak's check was not successful because her documents did not match the name on her Vinted account. We have since helped her update it, and her account is now verified."The company did not respond to the BBC's questions about the legal action Mali has taken and continues to pursue.Mangopay said it was "bound to professional secrecy and data protection obligations. We are, therefore, not allowed to comment on individual cases involving our clients or their users, nor can we share details about specific accounts, transactions or legal matters."

schema.headline: I took Vinted to court to get my money back

title: Spain v England: Nations League test will reveal if Thomas Tuchel has learned lessons
description: England's proof of progress and the lessons learned by head coach Thomas Tuchel since the disappointment of World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina w
body: England's proof of progress and the lessons learned by head coach Thomas Tuchel since the disappointment of World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina will be put to the sternest test when they face holders Spain in Madrid.Spain present the toughest assignment England could face, with the world champions' unbeaten run – in which they claimed the sport's biggest prize by beating Argentina in New Jersey in the summer – now stretching to 43 games.Luis de la Fuente's side last lost - to Colombia - in March 2024, winning 34 games and drawing nine in the intervening period, during which they also became European champions, beating England in the Euro 2024 final in Berlin.Little wonder, then, that England captain and Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane describes Sunday night's visit to the Metropolitano Stadium as: "The perfect opportunity to try and prove ourselves."Tuchel, who revealed Leeds United's James Trafford will get another opportunity in goal as he continues to alternate with Jordan Pickford, clearly feels the same as he added: "This will be proof of concept on the highest level. It's the biggest test in world football. Spain are unbelievable on an incredible run."Spain won the last big titles. We are trying to take it away from them. We are up for it. We are in a good moment to push our limits. We are up for something spectacular."It was a message echoed here in Madrid by England midfielder Declan Rice, who said: "It's a massive game."I don't think you can get much bigger than a Champions League final with Arsenal or a World Cup semi-final against Argentina, which I've played in, but when you are playing against the world champions in Spain there is no greater incentive."It's the sort of game that brings out the best in us. We want to play against the best teams and the best players. It will show where we are as a group. We're going to see where England are at."Spain are particularly formidable on home soil, unbeaten in 20 games - winning 15 and drawing five - since a 2-1 defeat by Switzerland in September 2022.England's most recent win in Spain was a 3-2 triumph in a Nations League encounter in Sevilla in October 2018, their first away victory against them for 31 years.Yet England came closer than most to piercing Spain's air of invincibility, even though they lost 3-2 at Wembley in September, when a rare Kane blemish from the penalty spot prevented them taking a potentially decisive 3-1 lead.Spain subsequently punished England and Kane, who will be hoping for better fortunes when the countries meet again in the latest Nations League encounter.England arrived in Madrid on Saturday evening having reeled off four successive victories since that Wembley loss, the latest of which was a 2-1 win against Croatia at Wembley on Thursday.Spain will present an altogether different opposition, but also a barometer of whether England have moved forward since the World Cup, when Tuchel was heavily criticised for what was perceived to be a negative approach in the 2-1 loss to Argentina in Atlanta, especially after Anthony Gordon put England ahead.Former England defender Matthew Upson, who will be in Madrid for BBC Radio 5 Live, told BBC Sport: "Harry Kane saying this is the perfect opportunity for England to prove themselves is a great way to build this challenge up."I wouldn't expect anything less from him considering where he is at now, where his belief level is and what he wants to achieve."Harry is achieving incredible personal accolades like the Ballon d'Or, but he won't rest there. He will want a team honour with England, and if you play against the best in the world there is no better barometer of where you're at as a group."It's going to be a very interesting test. It's fair to say we didn't see England at full flow against Croatia, so now we will see if they adjust, improve and produce something of their best, which they will have to do if you are going to get any sort of result against Spain in Spain."If England get a point, or even better a win, against Spain with their record, at home and away, we will come away thinking they are at a high level."If you get a result, you will have had to play really well because you won't do that with anything else."By that, I don't mean a blistering game. I just mean doing things well and showing the level you are at."In the aftermath of that World Cup loss to Argentina, the post-tournament process embarked upon by the Football Asssociation included canvassing the opinions of the whole squad, where it emerged it took place at a "full and frank" meeting with Tuchel at the start of the September international break.Kane and Jude Bellingham were understood to have given forthright views, where the approach in the devastating loss to Argentina was a key theme.There is now believed to be a feeling in the squad that Tuchel has taken on the lessons of Atlanta and is focusing on a more positive approach.Upson said: "England are still a bit of a work in progress. We have two or maybe three players who are playing some of the best football across Europe and the world at the moment. I am thinking of Kane, Bellingham and, at times, Anthony Gordon."The key is utilising that, then getting the rest of the team to a place where it can support that and deliver its own world-class support. This is the challenge for Thomas Tuchel.""England are adopting a more positive approach, but look a little vulnerable defensively, which is maybe the compromise."Yes, England could have been 3-1 up against Spain had Harry Kane scored his penalty, but don't forget we could easily have been 3-0 down before we scored."The intense environment of facing the World Cup holders on their own turf will also be a forensic examination of England's mental progress as well as footballing prowess.Upson said: "The biggest thing to fix after the World Cup was player reaction and player belief when we're in certain situations, especially if we go ahead and all of a sudden the game is difficult, as it was against Argentina. What is our mindset going to be?"Since then England have tried to play much more freely, openly and confidently. That's how I see it. That's how we played when we won 7-0 in Croatia. We were free, open, positive. Belief was through the roof."This is why this test against Spain is great because you will get tested to the maximum there. If England go ahead, let's see how they do and what they do. If they go behind, let's see what we do."Against Spain at Wembley, I saw a reaction at half-time from England, which was fantastic. We should have gone 3-1 up with Harry's penalty, and in that 15 minutes after half-time we were super positive, aggressive in our decision-making."This was another ideal situation to test that. They came through that really positively. It would be great if we get another test like that on Sunday."It it all plays into what Harry Kane said. This is something which will test people. It's a really significant game for England on a lot of levels."

schema.headline: Spain v England: Nations League test will reveal if Thomas Tuchel has learned lessons

title: Holly Humberstone on her identity crisis - and struggle being compared to other pop stars
description: Holly Humberstone: People can't connect to a pop star who's 'too polished'Image source, Silken WeinbergImage caption, Holly Humberstone says she was h
body: Holly Humberstone: People can't connect to a pop star who's 'too polished'Image source, Silken WeinbergImage caption, Holly Humberstone says she was having an identity crisis on a weekly basisByMusic correspondentYou might know her as a pop star, endorsed by everyone from Taylor Swift to Sam Fender, but Holly Humberstone has a secret double life. In her spare time, the singer-songwriter is literally a cat burglar."We've stolen one of our neighbours' cats by accident," she laughs, in a Zoom call from her fixer-upper in New Cross, south-east London. "He's a tiny little black cat who's come into our garden and simply chosen us."Under the slightest scrutiny, however, her story crumbles like a biscuit in a hot cup of tea."OK, we've been coercing him into the house with treats," she admits. "He's just so cute."But we're not trying to keep him. We literally push him out every night."Humberstone's excuse for this feline felony is that, last year, her parents sold her childhood home in Lincolnshire, external and moved to Wales  – taking her pets with them.One, a cat called Tsuki, had even been immortalised in the song Lucy as a confidante who listens to her problems but "never judges"."Oh, she knows some secrets!" laughs the singer. "I'm so glad she can't talk.""We actually tried to bring her to London with us, but she's a countryside cat and she hated it so much. We had to send her to Wales where she can be free and frolic."Her parents' relocation was disruptive for the human Humberstones, too. Their house, a "freezing cold, falling down" property 20 minutes outside of Grantham, played a huge part in the singer's success.Her early EPs were all written there, inspiring the "wonky sonics" of her indie-leaning pop sound. The 2021 single Haunted House is even dedicated to the "friendly" spirits who inhabited the property."It's a place I always felt I could go back to, to remind myself of who I am," she says. Instead, she spent 2025 "packing up 23 years of stuff my family and I had accumulated", from her old ballet shoes and poetry books to forgotten bits of jewellery.Image source, Holly HumberstoneImage caption, The singer shared photos of her old bedroom, and the artefacts she'd rediscovered, while clearing out her parents' "haunted house" in Grantham (pictured, left).The process was unsettling. Already grappling with the idea of leaving childhood behind, Humberstone found herself literally throwing away her past."I felt uprooted. I was having some sort of identity crisis almost weekly," she says.So she did what she's always done, and poured those feelings into her second album, Cruel World, which entered the UK charts at number four earlier this year."Writing these songs felt like building myself a little shield and a kind of safety bubble," she says. "There's an escapist, fantasy element to so much of the album."Maybe that's true, but Humberstone has always had the ability to locate a song's emotional core, and the lyrics on Cruel World don't disappoint."To lose somebody is to know you're only human, honey," she sings on To Love Somebody, external, soothing her elder sister as she endures an agonising break-up.Undeterred by that heartbreak, she throws herself headfirst into a new affair on Die Happy, external, declaring: "Hit the gas, I want it fast, want it reckless."But the most revealing song is the closing track, Beauty Pageant, external.Fragile and raw, it's the sound of Humberstone in her dressing room, addressing the woman in the mirror who'd "die for the applause" but who struggles with the impossible beauty standards imposed on female artists.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Humberstone's biggest songs include Falling Asleep At The Wheel, The Walls Are Way Too Thin, Die Happy and Scarlett"That's a song that I wasn't really setting out to write," she confesses."Writing about other people often feels easier than turning the magnifying glass on yourself."The lyrics, she says, draw on a "very specific" mindset she acquired at her all-girls school in Grantham."It was drilled into me: You're all in competition. You're only rewarded if you're the best. And if you're not, you're worthless."The experience "really warped the way I view other girls", she says.Musical success made it worse. After winning the Brits Rising Star award in 2022, Humberstone found herself competing with megastars, even though her music leaned towards the alternative side of pop."I'm a very small fish and I recognise that, but suddenly I was in meetings being compared to all these people on my label's roster, who are on a completely different scale," she says."It's something I really, really struggled with in the early days and it's something I've really had to unlearn."Nowadays, Humberstone has stopped benchmarking herself against her peers, recognising that the need for validation never fades."I don't think that there's a point I could get to, or an award that I could win, where these feelings would disappear," she says."Everybody feels like they've still got something to prove, so I'm done with setting myself goals - because then I lose sight of the real reason that I'm doing this, which is to write music that represents me, and have other people feel understood through that music."Image source, Silken WeinbergImage caption, "I pray that one day I'll turn and face the mirror with a smile," sings Humberstone That mindset comes to fruition in the new, expanded edition of Cruel World, whose five new songs were largely written after the original album was handed in."I was super proud of Cruel World and, when you've got that in your back pocket, there's room to experiment and break some of your usual parameters."The new tracks find Humberstone embracing a new persona – more confident, more flirtatious, a little salty – with music inspired by a playlist featuring Abba, Madonna and Robyn.The single Too Cute To Be Lonely, external is a will-they/won't-they story set at a house party."Don't leave a girl upset, in such a pretty dress," she teases the object of her affections.Terminally Yours takes place a couple of weeks later, when Humberstone realises she's fallen head-over-heels in love."Your stupid face is my sorry fate," she harrumphs, cross at herself.  "For [expletive]'s sake, I'm in love."Silver Sky, a gorgeous acoustic ballad, tells another side of the story, as she settles into her lover's arms and drifts into blissful reverie."I wrote that on a kind of Hail Mary trip, seeing what fell out of the air in Nashville," she reveals."We went over to [co-writer Maddie Diaz's] house, took a guitar into the garden and wrote Silver Sky outside, while all of these gorgeous red cardinals were singing around us."I usually write a lot about my mental health struggles, but I was just in the mood to write something that made me feel good."Image source, JME InternationalImage caption, Humberstone won the Brits Rising Star award in 2022, joining the ranks of former winners such as Sam Fender, Florence + The Machine and AdeleNot that her mental health issues are in the rear view mirror. Humberstone admits her stage nerves have only intensified since the release of Cruel World."It's the proudest I've been of any of my work and, for that reason, I struggled with shows because I felt a lot of pressure to go out and deliver it to the standard that I think people are expecting."But on the other hand, it's totally fine if you mess up or sing a wrong note. People can't connect to a pop star that feels too robotic and polished. "So maybe my strength is that vulnerability, and I need to recognise that more."That vulnerability has won Humberstone millions of fans, even if a hit single has (so far) eluded her. And her audience keeps growing.  In May this year, her breakout single Falling Asleep At The Wheel was awarded a silver disc... five years after its release, indicating that her songs have staying power in an era of disposable hits.Astonishingly, this is news to Humberstone, who learns about the accolade during our interview. But it helps to clarify a thought that's been knocking around her head."If I'm going to be doing this for years to come, I've just got to keep making music that feels right, trusting my gut and realising there's no end point," she says."Reaching an end point would mean I've 'made it', but I think, maybe, that's a myth that doesn't really exist."

schema.headline: Holly Humberstone on her identity crisis - and struggle being compared to other pop stars

title: Beauty advent calendars can cost hundreds - but are they value for money?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByLucy HookerDaniel Thomas and Faarea MasudBBC business reportersIt's easy to see the appeal of a beauty advent calendar. Li
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByLucy HookerDaniel Thomas and Faarea MasudBBC business reportersIt's easy to see the appeal of a beauty advent calendar. Like many women at this time of year, Julia says she often finds herself tempted to splurge on one - especially a perfume calendar. But she takes quite an unsentimental approach."I always look at what's in them. If I like enough of the fragrances, I'll buy it," says the 39-year old, who works as a senior commercial manager in engineering.Luxury advent calendars are supposed to offer the thrill of a surprise but, for Julia, it is more important she actually wants the items inside - a thought that is also striking more and more customers in the wake of the scandal over the Skims calendar.Image source, Getty Images/SkimsImage caption, Customers likened the contents of Kim Kardashian's Skims calendar to something you would find down the back of a sofaThis week, Kim Kardashian's beauty brand offered all of its customers refunds for its $148 (£110) calendar after being widely criticised on social media over the quality of its contents, with some customers likening the hair clips, scrunchies and keychains inside to things you might find down the back of a sofa.Julia says she earns a good salary but is keen to get value for money and doesn't want to waste it on items she won't use."I spent £160 on a Space NK fragrance calendar last year," she says. "I got some fragrances I'd been wanting for a while for a lot less than recommended retail price, and those I didn't like I managed to sell on for a slight mark-up on what I paid."Image source, SuppliedImage caption, Julia, 39, says she thinks fragrance calendars are usually good value for money  Beauty calendars, which often cost upwards of £100 and sometimes much more, have been around for more than a decade and the marketing has grown ever more sophisticated.High-profile brands will warn that their calendars risk running out, which may boost early demand, while unboxing videos posted by influencers can encourage spending by creating an infectious sense of surprise and delight. And it appears to be working. Ipsos data shows, external around 15% of all advent calendars sold are beauty ones, with people aged 18-34 particularly willing to splash out.But in the face of that tsunami of marketing, customers seem to be getting savvier."I love beauty, but I rarely buy beauty advent calendars. They are pricey and often only have a few things that I actually want to try or are trending products," says Priya Raj, 30, a fashion journalist.She thinks some are good value but, for her, the advantage is being able to try on a small scale without forking out for a full-size product."For me, an advent calendar - particularly a beauty one - serves the purpose of allowing me to try out different products, particularly in the lead-up to Christmas, and then I can hopefully snag a bargain in the Boxing Day sales."Image source, SuppliedImage caption, Priya Raj, 30, a fashion journalist, says the calendars "serve the purpose of allowing me to try out different products"Podcaster Rhea Somaiya, 28, also likes the general idea, but has a healthy scepticism around a lot of them in practice. "I do think some brands take the consumer for granted in that they provide each day with something so menial that people are bombarded with irrelevant and cluttering items. "And when that's the case, they certainly put me off as the excitement to open each window dwindles into irritation rather than joy."Image source, SuppliedImage caption, Podcaster Rhea Somaiya, 28, is less keen on the calendars and says they leave consumers "bombarded with irrelevant and cluttering items"Jessica Jasper, a marketing consultant, is more positive - she thinks it's worth it. But she also thinks some companies are just jumping on a trend and that "some brands are getting a little carried away with the pricing".So can beauty calendars offer value for both the brands and the customer - an example of a win-win? Or are they mainly designed to make us spend more at Christmas than we need to?Image source, SuppliedImage caption, "Some brands are getting a little carried away with the pricing," says marketing consultant Jessica JasperHeather Widdows, a philosophy professor and beauty expert, has pointed out that while you might buy some of the products in an advent calendar individually, it's highly unlikely you'd buy all of them.  "Beauty calendars may offer you lots of products for a really good price. They can also be a bit of fun and feel sensuous. "But it is exceptionally unlikely that you would use all the products inside them, so they're probably not worth it." This year, Julia has spent £99 on a John Lewis fragrance calendar which she thinks is good value for money. But it doesn't mean she'll keep everything in it.In fact she's joined a Facebook group where people trade the ones they don't want for ones they do. "The ones I keep are already a lot cheaper per mililitre than if you bought them at retail," she says.With additional reporting from Kris BramwellGet in touchHave you bought something you didn’t feel was value for money? Or seen misleading discounts on products?

schema.headline: Beauty advent calendars can cost hundreds - but are they value for money?

title: Judo champion Teddy Riner shakes up French presidential race with surprise candidacy
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Five-times Olympic champion Teddy Riner is one of France's most popular athletesByHugh SchofieldIn ParisApart from
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Five-times Olympic champion Teddy Riner is one of France's most popular athletesByHugh SchofieldIn ParisApart from an overwhelming urge to pin one's opponent to the floor of the house, there is no obvious connection between politics and the world of top-level judo.That has not stopped France's much-garlanded world heavyweight champion Teddy Riner from throwing his hat into the ring for next April's presidential race.The Guadeloupe-born 37-year-old may have no experience of public office, no party behind him, and as yet no manifesto. All so far is a slogan La France qu'on aime (The France we love), a declaration on social media, and a campaign visit to a hospital in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris.But it would be a foolhardy pundit who would totally write off his chances.Riner is, after all, one of the most popular figures in modern-day France, regularly topping the polls for embodying the nation's "values". He is a proven winner, with five Olympic golds and 11 world championships under his belt, as well as a successful career in business.More than 28 million people have watched his election broadcast on Instagram and X, shot with proper presidential decorum against a backdrop of books and a French flag. Some 22% told an Ifop poll within 24 hours they "could" vote for him.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Teddy Riner's video has attracted 14.5 million views on Instagram aloneActors and television personalities have become presidents in other countries. The ex-leader of Liberia – George Weah – was formerly a professional footballer.So why not a judoka in the Élysée Palace?"Anyone who thinks that being out of the political in-crowd disqualifies Riner from running for the Élysée would be very wrong," says Guillaume Tabard of Le Figaro."But [Riner] too would be wrong if he thinks not belonging to the in-crowd is all it takes."For now the whole of the French political world has decided to take the Riner candidacy seriously – or at least to pretend to. That is partly because he is such a popular personality that mocking his political hopes could easily rebound badly.But it is also because the state of French politics – outside of the burgeoning forces of the hard left and hard right – is one of total disarray.The centre-ground is floundering, with no candidate yet emerging who can inspire anything like the sense of mission of hard-right leader Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon on the hard left, who for now look set to face off in the final round of the presidential election in May.So when a popular figure like Riner enters the race - proclaiming himself "neither left, nor right", wanting to "unite the country" and "put money back in people's pockets", railing equally against "racists" and "yobs who scare people off our streets" – politicians have to take note.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Hard-right leader Marine Le Pen currently leads the polls in the race to be France's next presidentIt is perfectly possible, probable even, that Riner's campaign will fizzle out after a brief period of hype, and that the judoka will after all be a joker in the pack. But it is also possible that it won't, in which case the pre-election arithmetic will need a hasty readjustment: and it won't be the centrists who are smiling.Thus far, Riner has shown himself a master of the codes required for this kind of out-of-nowhere candidacy, the first of which is to press home the message: "Don't Worry! I'm NOT a Politician!"In this day and age in France, anyone who smacks of the "system" is automatically downgraded in voters' eyes, so it is important to emphasise that you are only running for office because, one, you have experienced real life (unlike those loafers in Paris); and two, you have discovered that there are solutions out there for the country's many problems. Solutions that are invisible to those same blinkered apparatchiks.All this Riner was able to express in last Monday's social media broadcast by using sophisticated rhetorical devices."People say I am a fool for wanting to run for the presidency," he said."Am I a fool? Well, if refusing to see France sink under the weight of debt; refusing to see mothers and fathers grit their teeth every time they do their weekly shop, and tremble with fear when their kids go out on the street… if all that means being a fool, then yes call me a fool."It was a promising oratorial start for the sportsman, and certainly attracted the viewers. But if he is serious – and Riner says he never does anything half-heartedly - that's not how he became an Olympic champion – then the hard work begins now.What does Riner actually want to do? Who will be on his team? Where does he position himself on the all-consuming matters of the day: pension-reform,  investment in education, the cost of living, public debt, the rise of populism or Russia's war in Ukraine?In short, how does he intend to transform his undeniable popularity as a sporting figure into a political mandate?Image source, ReutersImage caption, Protesters have for weeks taken to the streets in France over wages, the cost of living and public services Broadly, Riner appears to be on the right on economic matters and law and order, but being black and of Caribbean background he is also very strong on racism. When he says he is anti-extremism, he is referring mainly to Marine Le Pen.In other words his pitch is somewhere in the centre, and against the extremes.The trouble is, this is already an extremely crowded area, with important figures like ex-prime ministers Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal signally failing to take off.Currently there are a dozen or so candidates in the area between centre right and centre left, stretching from the Socialist-backed Raphaël Glucksman to the Republicans' Bruno Retailleau on the right.The latest possible addition is Christine Lagarde, who steps down as head of the European Central Bank next February.Image source, Pool/AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, President Emmanuel Macron is among the few politicians who appears genuinely pleased by Riner's decision to runThe addition of yet another contender will dilute their polling numbers even further, making a second-round qualification for Mélenchon more likely.So no wonder the leader of France Unbowed (LFI) seemed so happy about Riner's decision to run. "We know how it goes: neither right nor left means not left," Mélenchon told reporters on Friday.The only other politician who seems genuinely pleased, rather than putting on a fixed smile, is President Emmanuel Macron, who said Riner was a "great champion" and that politics "did not belong to the professionals".That could be explained by the president's cool relations with his former prime ministers, Philippe and Attal, both of whom are doing all they can to distance themselves from their unpopular one-time boss.Riner said he viewed Macron's praise as a "poisoned chalice", telling reporters on Saturday that he was "not the president's envoy, I'm not a Macronist".Politics and judo have very little in common, but of the two, as Riner will soon discover, the more vicious is not the one that is fought out hand-to-hand after mutual acknowledgement on the tatami mat. In Japanese, judo actually means "the gentle way".If he starts looking like a serious candidate, Riner must know his life will be turned upside down, not just his physical form. In politics you do not bow in respect to your opponent. You give him a metaphorical headbutt.

schema.headline: Judo champion Teddy Riner shakes up French presidential race with surprise candidacy

title: Handwritten 200-year-old dismissal letter found on Rugeley roof tile
description: Image source, CawardenImage caption, The message reads: "I do hereby discharge you, John Lewis, from my employment, Thomas Austin."ByRichard PriceWest
body: Image source, CawardenImage caption, The message reads: "I do hereby discharge you, John Lewis, from my employment, Thomas Austin."ByRichard PriceWest MidlandsWhat appears to be a 200-year-old letter of dismissal, written on a roof slate,  has been found at a salvage yard.The tile, informing what is thought to be a 19th-century pottery worker that he was no longer needed, was found at Cawarden Reclaim in Rugeley, Staffordshire.The message had been written into soft clay before the Staffordshire Blue tile was fired, and reads: "I do hereby discharge you, John Lewis, from my employment, Thomas Austin."Research had found a firm called Thomas Austin Brick & Tile Makers, based at Clay Hills, Stoke-on-Trent in 1820, which could be the business referenced on the tile, the firm said."We were looking around and we just happened to come across this tile," said general manager Adam Giles.He said he brought it back to his yard, cleaned it up a bit, and immediately felt it had a historic significance.Image source, Cawarden ReclaimImage caption, The Staffordshire Blue roof tile announces the dismissal of worker John LewisThe name, location and period made a fascinating potential connection, the company said, but conceded they did not know for certain that the two were linked."If it is the same person [Thomas Austin], we may have uncovered not only a glimpse into somebody's working life in the early 19th century, but also a connection to the people who made the very building materials that have survived to this day," Giles said."You come across quite a few pawprints from animals and old shoes, where they used to walk across the clay while they were being fired," he said."You see that, but not very often you see handwritten text in a tile. Very unusual, very rare."Image source, Cawarden ReclaimImage caption, The tile has been weathered by about 200 years spent on a roofOnce the inscription had been made, the clay was fired to create a finished roof tile and was then put to its intended use."The fact that someone went to the trouble of writing that out on the back of clay before it was fired, and then firing the tile and using it for the purpose it was designed for," Giles added.The company said intriguing items such as this were uncovered from time to time, and that they were kept aside and preserved when they were found.Eventually, they would go on display in the firm's reception area as part of a wall of interest, they said.Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Staffordshire

schema.headline: Handwritten 200-year-old dismissal letter found on Rugeley roof tile

title: Thousands turn out in Edinburgh to protest against AI data centres
description: Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, Protesters marched down the Royal Mile towards the Scottish Parliament ByMary McCoolBBC Scotland NewsTho
body: Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, Protesters marched down the Royal Mile towards the Scottish Parliament ByMary McCoolBBC Scotland NewsThousands of people have joined a protest in Edinburgh against the building of large-scale AI data centres.Demonstrators with placards - and some dressed in costume - assembled at the top of the Royal Mile before marching towards the Scottish Parliament.The event comes at a time of widespread debate about the environmental impact of data centres and is part of a wave of protests across Europe.The Scottish government will soon publish new planning guidance on data centres and said it was developing a strategy to maximise the "public benefit".Image source, Getty ImagesImage source, Press AssociationImage caption, Some demonstrators attended in eye-catching costume to draw attention to particular issuesImage source, Press AssociationInnovation Minister Alyn Smith recently said data centres were "the whisky bonds of the AI sector".However protesters made it clear they disagree - carrying slogans such as "AI data centres threaten humanity" and "AI data centres: costing the Earth".Some attended to voice their opposition to plans for data centres in particular communities - including Cockenzie, East Lothian, and Larbert, Falkirk.Kim Cairns, a campaigner for 'Say No To Chapelcross AI Data Centre', told BBC Scotland News her community was worried about noise, road closures and access problems during the construction phase.She was also concerned about the noise the centre would generate when it was operational.Kim said: "It's not going to enrich anybody's lives. For Chapelcross it's the sheer size of it, the amount of electricity it's going to need."At the moment it's green fields with sheep and cows in it. It's going to be a monstrosity on the environment. "The air pollution, the light pollution - it's just not needed."Image source, Press AssociationImage source, Press AssociationAI is seen by some as the most transformative technology ever made but others have warned there is chance that if the frightening pace of development continues it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.Meanwhile, Scotland's data centre debate centres around the scale and impact of the sites themselves.At the moment, the biggest data centre in Scotland is thought to be DataVita's site in Airdrie, North Lanarkshire, which has a capacity for 12MW.But if one planned for Chapelcross, Dumfries and Galloway, goes ahead it will have a capacity of 1,000MW - making it one of the largest data centres in the world.The Scottish Greens and campaign groups have called for a moratorium on large data centres, arguing they could undermine climate targets and place additional pressure on renewable energy supplies.The innovation minister previously told BBC Scotland some of the discourse around the subject was "wild".Smith said: "You'd think there wasn't a planning system at all. "Comparing a really bad data centre in the middle of the Utah desert doesn't track through to what we're going to have in Scotland."Figure caption, Thousands turn out in Edinburgh to protest against AI data centresFriends of the Earth campaigner Kim Pratt believes the people of Scotland should have the final say on the building of data centres.She said: "The way that these data centres are being proposed is going to make a lot of profit for big tech companies but they're going to have huge impacts for people in Scotland."These developments are so massive they're going to have national-level impacts -they're energy hungry developments. "There would be a massive increase in our energy bills but also in terms of climate impact as well."The Scottish government is only taking a few months to consider these impacts - and these developments are so new, we don't know what all the impacts will be."Scotcast: AI and data centres: what now?15 SeptemberThe Scottish government confirmed it would publish new planning guidance on data centres before the end of the year and was "developing a strategic approach to maximising the public benefit from data centres located in Scotland".A spokesperson added: "Planning authorities are also now required to notify ministers of new data centre applications, with a new planning direction also mandating an Environmental Impact Assessment to be submitted during planning for all new data centres with a power capacity exceeding 50 megawatts."

schema.headline: Thousands turn out in Edinburgh to protest against AI data centres

title: Judge temporarily blocks Trump from closing Washington DC golf course for renovation
description: A federal judge has temporarily blocked the US government's closure of a historic golf course and park in Washington DC. US District Judge Ana Reyes h
body: A federal judge has temporarily blocked the US government's closure of a historic golf course and park in Washington DC. US District Judge Ana Reyes has been overseeing a months-long challenge to the president's plans for East Potomac Golf Links, which he said would be closed from 15 November for extensive renovations.Reyes has said Donald Trump cannot close the park or its golf course, but added that his administration was not required to actively manage either.Trump, an avid golfer, has said his plans to upgrade the 106-year-old course will create "one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World". The BBC has contacted the White House for comment. Declaring the current course "Trash Island", he announced in October it would be renovated over 15 months to create a space that "will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments" - despite the ongoing litigation.In a 30-page decision issued on Saturday, Reyes said the Trump administration's justifications for the proposed course closures were pretextual, and that the government violated at least two federal laws "to meet an arbitrary deadline.""The Government proposes to close a historic park, daily enjoyed by Washingtonians of all stripes, indefinitely," Reyes wrote.She said the closure "runs counter to the public interest in utilising national parkland", adding that the government had not "plausibly identified any harm it would suffer from a temporary restraining order that preserves the status quo pending further proceedings".Her order will last until the 28 November.The legal dispute dates back to February, when the DC Preservation League and others sued over redevelopment plans for the park.The historic course, which sits 2 miles (3km) south of the White House, is one of three public courses run by the National Park Service in the nation's capital.The legal fight then escalated in October, when the NPS began to cut down hundreds of trees without notifying Reyes until 15 hours before work was set to begin. After the trees were cut, Reyes ordered the Trump administration to stop tree removal until at least 26 October and give her three business days' notice about making any other permanent changes. Despite the work stoppage, Trump announced that the course would be closed for 15 months from 15 November to accommodate the renovations. He also shared a rendering of the course redesign."The current Course is old, broken, dilapidated, and of no further use or effect. It is in very poor condition, with falling, dangerous, and disease-infested trees and, importantly, a collapsing and hazardous seawall," he said in a post to Truth Social.Reyes has since separately opened an inquiry into whether the justice department attorneys "have made misrepresentations to the court and otherwise violated ethical rules".That included whether giving late notice to the court about the renovation plans was "done in bad faith" and whether the attorneys failed to correct previously false statements or withheld information.She said she would carry out the inquiry with a special master, an independent third party.

schema.headline: Judge temporarily blocks Trump from closing Washington DC golf course for renovation
